blocks.html: SQL (Structured Query Language) is the standard language for working with relational databases. With SQL you tell the DBMS what you want, and it decides how to get it. That is why SQL is called a declarative language: you do not write loops as you would in C++.
In this chapter we use MySQL, a free, open-source and widely used relational DBMS. You can type SQL commands at the mysql> prompt in the MySQL command-line client, or in MySQL Workbench.

items.html: SQL keywords are not case-sensitive: SELECT , select and Select all work. This book writes keywords in capitals for clarity.
Every statement ends with a semicolon ; .
Text and dates go inside single quotes: 'Patna' , '2026-11-03' .
A statement may run over several lines.
Comments start with -- (followed by a space) or are enclosed in /* ... */ .

blocks.html: CHAR vs VARCHAR: CHAR(10) always uses 10 characters of space and pads shorter text with spaces. VARCHAR(10) uses only as much space as the text needs (plus a little overhead). Use CHAR for fixed codes such as 'M' , 'F' or '12A' , and VARCHAR for names and addresses.
A constraint is a rule on a column that the DBMS enforces on every insert and update (Chapter 8).

rows: The column cannot be left empty
No two rows can have the same value
The value used when none is given
The value must exist in the referenced table's primary key
Values must satisfy the condition (enforced from MySQL 8.0.16 onwards)

blocks.code:
CREATE TABLE STUDENT (
    RollNo  INT PRIMARY KEY,
    Name    VARCHAR(30) NOT NULL,
    Class   CHAR(3),
    Gender  CHAR(1),
    Marks   INT CHECK (Marks BETWEEN 0 AND 100),
    City    VARCHAR(20) DEFAULT 'Patna'
);

CREATE TABLE FEES (
    ReceiptNo INT PRIMARY KEY,
    RollNo    INT,
    Month     VARCHAR(10),
    Amount    DECIMAL(8,2),
    FOREIGN KEY (RollNo) REFERENCES STUDENT(RollNo)
);

DESCRIBE STUDENT;    -- shows the structure (also written as DESC STUDENT;)

ALTER TABLE STUDENT ADD Phone CHAR(10);             -- add a column
ALTER TABLE STUDENT MODIFY Name VARCHAR(40);        -- change a column's type
ALTER TABLE STUDENT DROP Phone;                     -- remove a column
ALTER TABLE STUDENT RENAME COLUMN City TO Town;     -- rename (MySQL 8)
ALTER TABLE FEES ADD UNIQUE (RollNo, Month);        -- add a constraint

rows: SELECT Name, Marks FROM STUDENT WHERE Marks > 80;

Vikas

blocks.html: BETWEEN 80 AND 90 includes both 80 and 90.
NULL means "unknown", so Marks = NULL never matches anything. Use IS NULL or IS NOT NULL .

blocks.code:
SELECT Name FROM STUDENT WHERE Marks IS NULL;        -- Neha
SELECT Name FROM STUDENT WHERE Marks IS NOT NULL;    -- the other 5
SELECT Name, Marks FROM STUDENT ORDER BY Marks DESC;

items.html: ASC (ascending) is the default. DESC gives descending order.
MySQL treats NULL as the smallest value, so it comes first in ASC order and last in

blocks.html: DESC order.

items.html: Sort on two columns: ORDER BY Class, Marks DESC (by class first, then the highest marks first within each class).

blocks.html: Compare with Chapter 5: this one line does the work of a whole C++ sorting program.
A single-row function works on each row and gives one result per row.

blocks.code: SELECT UPPER(Name), LENGTH(Name) FROM STUDENT WHERE Class = '12A';

blocks.html: An aggregate function works on many rows and gives one result. All of them except
COUNT(*) ignore NULL values.

blocks.code:
SELECT COUNT(*), COUNT(Marks), SUM(Marks), AVG(Marks), MAX(Marks), MIN(Marks)
FROM STUDENT;

blocks.html: COUNT(*) counts all 6 rows. COUNT(Marks) counts only the 5 rows where Marks is not
NULL. AVG = 407 / 5 = 81.4, because Neha's NULL is left out and not counted as 0.
GROUP BY puts rows with the same value into groups, and an aggregate function then
runs on each group.
For 12A, (78 + 92 + 64) / 3 = 78. For 12B, (85 + 88) / 2 = 86.5, because Neha's NULL is ignored.
HAVING filters groups, just as WHERE filters rows.

blocks.code: SELECT ... FROM ... WHERE ... GROUP BY ... HAVING ... ORDER BY ...;
SELECT * FROM STUDENT, FEES;

In the Python book, mysql.connector links Python to MySQL. In C++ we use MySQL Connector/C++, the official library from MySQL. Its classic (JDBC-style) API works in four steps:

items.html: Connect to the MySQL server with a host, user name and password.
Choose the database (schema).
Run an SQL statement: executeQuery() for SELECT, executeUpdate() for INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE.
Read the result row by row with ResultSet::next() , then close the connection.
Install the MySQL Server and MySQL Connector/C++ (on Ubuntu, for example: sudo apt install libmysqlcppconn-dev ; on Windows, use the MySQL Installer).
Compile with the library linked: g++ student_db.cpp -o student_db - lmysqlcppconn

Header paths: older packages use #include <mysql_driver.h> and #include <cppconn/...> . Connector/C++ 8.x and later installs them as #include <jdbc/mysql_driver.h> and #include <jdbc/cppconn/...> . Use the form that matches your installation.
